settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: A per-user random 16-byte salt is applied before hashing (Credential.randomSalt and Credential.hash), which defeats precomputed rainbow tables and makes identical passwords hash differently across users.
Digest comparison uses Credential.byteEquals, which checks length and avoids early-exit sequencing, mitigating online timing attacks on the comparison even though offline cracking cost is unaffected.

The reviewed files show no configurable iteration count or KDF, but the absence of such configuration in these two files does not prove none exists elsewhere in the repository (e.g. enterprise security code or a migration routine).
candidates.description: Credential.forPassword(int) generates a 16-byte random salt and stores the digest of SHA-256 over (salt || UTF-8 password), with DIGEST_ALGO = SHA-256 used directly. This is a fast-hash, no-key-stretching scheme: a single SHA-256 invocation is evaluated per candidate password, so offline brute-force/dictionary attacks against a leaked auth store are cheap compared to PBKDF2/bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 with an iteration/work factor. The per-user salt prevents rainbow-table reuse and identical-hash reuse, and Credential.byteEquals performs a length-checked, non-early-exit comparison of the stored and computed digest, so an online timing oracle against the comparison is largely mitigated. The root issue is the absence of a key-derivation work factor in the reviewed code, not the presence of a logic bug. A secondary point in the same code: randomSalt() fills the salt using ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextBytes(salt). java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom is not a cryptographically secure generator; 16 bytes drawn from it are not a predictable constant, but salt uniqueness/unpredictability may be weaker than a SecureRandom-backed salt would provide. Note the digest field is also used for the legacy/unsupported password case, which appears to compare only the literal 'unsupported' value, a separate and not security-relevant path. These are storage-strength leads; no runtime exploitation is demonstrated or claimed.
missing_evidence: Whether any other code path upgrades stored credentials to a stronger KDF or migrates legacy hashes on login.
Whether deployment/operational guidance treats the credential store as a high-value secret equivalent to a key.
Concrete measurement that cracking the single-SHA-256 scheme is feasible in the intended threat model (no benchmark was executed).
The exact set of roles/paths allowed to read the credential store file.
preconditions: An attacker obtains a copy of the auth/credential store (backup, disk image, or read access to the file holding the hashed credentials).

The stored hash is reachable in the form written by Credential.forPassword (single SHA-256 over salt||password), i.e. no external upgrade to a stronger KDF is applied before or during cracking attempts.
candidates.title: Password credentials stored with a fast single-iteration SHA-256 and non-CSPRNG salt

counter_evidence: Both methods are ordinary administrative operations that are expected to be access-controlled; no bypass of those controls is shown in the reviewed lines.
Reaching these methods required no privileged or unusual path in the code read; they are the normal creation/update flows.
candidates.description: BasicAuthManager.newUser(String,String,String,String[]) builds a User with Credential.forPassword(initialPassword) (around lines 139-154), and setUserPassword(String,String) updates auth via users.setUserPassword(user, Credential.forPassword(newPassword)) (around lines 191-217). These are the runtime entry points that reach the hashing routine analysed in the Credential candidate: on user creation and on password change, credentials are stored using the single-iteration SHA-256 plus random salt scheme. This candidate documents reachability of the weak-work-factor storage scheme rather than an independent defect. It does not by itself establish anything about authorisation of these operations; those checks live in the surrounding code that was only partially read. Reported as a supporting reachability lead with the storage scheme's weaknesses as the underlying issue.
missing_evidence: Whether the auth store written here is protected by file permissions or encryption at rest.
Whether these methods are gated by an authorisation check in code outside the read spans (only partial reads of this file were available).
Any migration path that rewrites existing hashes to a stronger algorithm.
preconditions: A caller is authorised to create a user or change a user password on the server.
The account's credentials are later stored in the auth store and, per the Credential candidate, subject to offline attack if that store leaks.
candidates.title: Credential creation and password update paths invoke the fast-hash scheme in BasicAuthManager
